value: under high nutrient availability, A. negundo seedling growth rate (relative height growth rate) was 13 times higher in full light and shade (25 percent light), on average, than in deep shade (7 percent light)
method: experimental light contrast: greenhouse shade trial with thermal cloths over the plants giving full light (100 percent of ambient radiation, the control), shade (25 percent) and deep shade (7 percent), crossed with fertilisation (complete fertiliser on days 3, 14 and 53 or none) and disturbance (25 percent partial defoliation on days 21 and 48 or none); split-split-plot design (shade main plot, fertilisation subplot, disturbance sub-subplot) with 3 complete random blocks; four individuals per species randomly assigned to each of the 12 treatments, 720 individuals in total across five species; endpoint relative height growth rate (RGRh)
conditions: treatments 1 April to 14 June 2005 in 4 L pots; greenhouse air temperature set at 25 C day and 15 C night; the shade levels are given as percentages of ambient radiation and the Methods as read print no light measurement under the cloths and no under-cloth microclimate, so shade is a cloth treatment bundle, not an isolated irradiance effect; A. negundo seed collected fall 2003 along the Garonne River, sown spring 2004; the 13-fold figure holds only under high nutrient availability and averages full light and shade; Figure 1 means are of nine to twelve seedlings (+/- 1 SE); same subsection: shade (p = 0.0116) and shade x fertilisation (p = 0.0155) significant for A. negundo RGRh, fertilisation p = 0.0013, disturbance not significant (Table 1, 0.471); the same light and nutrient changes raised RGRh only 1.23 and 1.5 times in the early- and late-successional natives (Fraxinus excelsior, F. angustifolia, Populus nigra, Salix alba), and light affected only A. negundo; no separate test of the fertilised full-light against deep-shade contrast

source.authors: Porté AJ, Lamarque LJ, Lortie CJ, Michalet R, Delzon S
source.title: Invasive Acer negundo outperforms native species in non-limiting resource environments due to its higher phenotypic plasticity

where: Results, growth rate subsection (the sentence beginning 'To sum up' and ending '[...] early- and late-successional native species, respectively.'); p values from the same subsection; design from Methods
quote: To sum up, [...] A. negundo growth rate was 13 times higher in full light and shade (on average) compared to the deep shade level (Figure 1) under high nutrient availability, [...]
note: Growth endpoint in a set-light (shade-cloth) comparison, filed under sense_light_nonvisual by the plant ruling (LIGHT-RESPONSE.md basis: experimental light contrast); full light is the control level; the result is conditional on fertilisation (significant shade x fertilisation interaction). The opening cut drops the clause on 9.6-fold growth-rate plasticity relative to natives; the trailing cut drops the native-species comparison, given in conditions. value: receiver response to plant odour: adult fungus gnats preferred non-infected white clover plants (67 percent) over plants infected with White clover mosaic virus (33 percent)
method: odour-only receiver choice: closed-system Y-tube olfactometer, three pots of cuttings of one treatment in a 5-l glass cuvette at the upwind end of each arm, 4 l min-1 charcoal-filtered air per arm; one adult female Bradysia sp. released downwind and watched up to 10 min; 8 to 10 females per replicate pair of plant sets, seven sets, each gnat and plant used once; six non-choosers excluded; 24 C; chi-square test. Separate emitter assay: whole-plant headspace (80 min, Tenax TA and Carbopack B) of four grouped cuttings inoculated on the first two fully expanded leaves 4 days earlier, 13 replicate samplings per treatment against mock-inoculated (buffer only) controls, GC and canonical discriminant analysis
conditions: emitter: white clover (Trifolium repens), all experiments with cuttings of a single genotype (A120); receiver: adult female fungus gnats printed only as Bradysia sp.; olfactometer plants inoculated 18 and 3 days before testing (first and second replicate sets), volatile-sampling plants 4 days, and the two assays used separately prepared plants, so no volatiles were measured from the plants the gnats chose between; chi-square 4.84, p = 0.0278; infected and control blends differed (Cohen's kappa 0.9231, p < 0.0001) and beta-caryophyllene was detected only in infected plants' headspace, but no isolated or synthetic compound was tested on gnats, so which compounds drive the choice is untested; the abstract reports only marginal effects of infection on the larva-clover interaction; virus infection cut total biomass by 27 percent and gnat larvae by 52 percent (Results)

source.authors: van Molken T, de Caluwe H, Hordijk CA, Leon-Reyes A, Snoeren TAL, van Dam NM, Stuefer JF
source.title: Virus infection decreases the attractiveness of white clover plants for a non-vectoring herbivore

where: Results, adult fungus gnat choice test (sentence before the chi-square sentence); Methods, choice tests and volatile collection; Results, 'Virus-induced changes in plant volatile emission'
quote: These adults clearly preferred non-infected plants (67 %) over virus-infected plants (33 %), the preference being expressed as a percentage choice for either one of the two plant groups.
note: Filed under sense_chemical by the 10(a) signalling allowance (CHEMICAL-EVIDENCE.md): living emitter (white clover) and defined receiver (adult female Bradysia sp.), with the chemical connection shown by an odour-only olfactometer choice; the clover is the emitter, not a measured receiver, and the measured endpoint is the gnat's choice. The virus-induced change in emission alone is induced emission under a pathogen, not a chemical stimulus, and would not by itself qualify for sense_chemical. 'Signal' in an evolved sense is not claimed: odour-based avoidance of infected plants by a non-vector herbivore.
